title: Observability
summary: Metrics, logs and traces: how to find out what’s wrong, where, and why — fast.

goals.text: Why “it’s slow” is hard to debug
Handling an incident, and the post-mortem

steps.title: “Checkout is slow.” Where?
body: Support tickets pile up: checkout takes several seconds. A checkout touches the gateway, orders, inventory, payments, a database and a third-party fraud API.
You can see a request waiting somewhere in this diagram — but the team can’t. Every server’s CPU looks fine, and nobody knows where to start.

callout.text: If users find problems before you do, you are flying blind.

steps.title: Metrics: numbers over time
body: Every service records a few numbers about the requests it handles — the RED method: Rate (requests/s), Errors (failed share) and Duration (latency percentiles) — and sends them to a time-series store with dashboards.
Now the picture is clear: inventory and the database are fast; the slowness lives on the payments path.

callout.text: Common stacks: Prometheus + Grafana, Datadog, CloudWatch. Measure p99, not just averages. RED describes requests; for machines, watch USE: utilization, saturation, errors.

steps.title: Alert on what users feel
body: Don’t page people for “CPU above 80%” — it fires constantly and often means nothing. Alert on symptoms users feel.
Pick an SLI (say, the share of checkouts faster than 1 s), set an SLO target (99.9%), and alert when you’re burning through the remaining error budget too fast.

callout.text: An error budget turns reliability into a shared number: while it lasts, ship features; when it’s gone, fix reliability first.

steps.title: Logs: the story, line by line
body: Metrics say where; logs say what happened. Each service writes timestamped events — but at thousands of requests a second, lines from different requests interleave into noise.
The trick: give every request an id at the gateway, pass it along, and include it in every log line. Filter by one id and you get one request’s story.

callout.text: Log structured JSON, not free text — so you can filter by request id, user, service or status.

changes: + Request id on every log line

steps.title: Traces: follow one request everywhere
body: A distributed trace records every hop of one request as a span with a start time and duration, all joined by the same trace id. Drawn as a waterfall, it shows exactly where the time goes.
Follow the violet request: 2.1 of its 2.4 seconds are spent waiting for the third-party fraud API.

callout.text: Tools: OpenTelemetry to collect, Jaeger, Tempo, Honeycomb or Datadog to explore. Instrument once, use everywhere.

changes: ~ Cause found: fraud API ≈ 88% of the time

steps.title: Fix it, then prove it
body: With the cause known, the fix is quick: call the fraud API with a 300 ms timeout, cache recent scores, and review the rare slow cases afterwards.
The same dashboards prove it worked: p99 drops from 2.4 s to 310 ms, and the SLO alert clears. Total time from page to cause: minutes, not hours.

callout.text: Metrics tell you something is wrong, traces show where, logs explain why. You need all three.

changes: + 300 ms timeout + cache on fraud checks

steps.title: Case: 3 a.m. — errors spike
body: The pager fires: checkout errors jumped from 0.1% to 6% at 03:12. Inventory is the culprit on the dashboard. The deploy log shows a config change to inventory at 03:10.
Good practice is to mitigate first: roll the change back and restore service, and investigate the root cause afterwards — not the other way round.

callout.text: Put deploys and config changes on your dashboards as markers. “What changed?” is the first question in almost every incident.

steps.title: Learn from it: the post-mortem
body: After the incident, the team writes a post-mortem: a timeline, the impact, the root cause, and the actions that stop it happening again.
It’s blameless — the question is how the system let a mistake through, not who made it. Here: config changes now go through the same canary rollout as code.

callout.text: Each incident is expensive training data. Teams that write good post-mortems make the same mistake much less often.

changes: + Action: canary rollout for config too

card.title: Post-mortem · checkout errors
lines: cause: bad timeout in inventory config

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Metrics (rate, errors, duration) show where it hurts.
  • Alert on SLOs — what users feel — not on raw CPU.
  • Logs with a request id tell one request’s story.
  • Traces follow a request across every service.
  • In an incident, mitigate first; then write a blameless post-mortem.
Instrument before you need it — the outage is the wrong time to add logging.

callout.text: That completes Reliability. Next module: Architecture — starting with monoliths vs microservices.
